title: Nietzsche
orientation: Russell treats Nietzsche as Schopenhauer's more consistent successor: where Schopenhauer made will metaphysically fundamental but ethically evil, Nietzsche gives will both metaphysical and ethical primacy, producing an unapologetically aristocratic ethic centered on the 'noble' man and hostile to Christianity, democracy, socialism, and sympathy for the weak. This is one of the most polemical chapters in the book: Russell reconstructs Nietzsche's ethics and critique of religion in some detail, stages an extended imagined debate between Nietzsche and the Buddha, and closes by declaring his own side in that debate -- against Nietzsche -- in unusually direct, first-person terms.
historical_background: Nietzsche (1844-1900) was the son of a Protestant pastor and had a pious upbringing; a brilliant classical philologist, he became a professor at Basel in 1869 before taking his degree, was forced to retire in 1879 due to ill health, and lived out his remaining sane years in Swiss health resorts before becoming permanently insane in 1888 until his death. Russell notes his passionate admiration for, and later bitter break with, Wagner (ostensibly over the Christian renunciation of Parsifal), and situates Nietzsche's outlook within the wider nineteenth-century reception of Napoleon as romantic symbol, tracing his affinities to Byron (discussed two chapters earlier) and comparing his political philosophy at length to Machiavelli's.
philosophical_problems: Should ethics be aristocratic -- concerned only with the excellence of a superior few -- or democratic/universalist, treating the happiness or well-being of all persons as mattering?
Is sympathy/compassion a virtue rooted in genuine love, or (as Nietzsche claims) a symptom of fear and weakness dressed up as virtue?
What is the proper relationship between religion (specifically Christianity) and social order -- does Christian 'slave morality' protect the weak, or does it maliciously break the strong?
Can an ethical system that says 'good' really means what is desired by, or serves the interests of, a particular individual or type of person claim any objective or universal authority?

philosophers_discussed.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's primary subject: his life, his relationship to Schopenhauer and to Greek philosophy, his ethics of the 'noble man' and will to power, his contempt for women, his critique of Christianity as 'slave morality,' and his comparison to Machiavelli are all reconstructed, followed by Russell's extended critical evaluation.

philosophers_discussed.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented as Nietzsche's acknowledged predecessor, whose ethic of renunciation Nietzsche judged inconsistent with his own metaphysic of the omnipotence of will; Nietzsche is said to give will ethical as well as metaphysical primacy, correcting what he saw as Schopenhauer's incoherence.

philosophers_discussed.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Compared at length to Nietzsche: both hold an ethic that aims at power and is deliberately anti-Christian, though Machiavelli was a practical man of affairs while Nietzsche was 'an essentially bookish man' consciously opposed to the dominant trends of his time; what Caesar Borgia was to Machiavelli, Napoleon was to Nietzsche.

philosophers_discussed.name: Socrates and Plato
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Criticized by Nietzsche for their supposed democratic moral bias and taste for edification; Nietzsche cannot forgive Socrates his humble origin, calling him a 'roturier,' and suggests Plato may have preached virtue only as a means of controlling the lower classes.

philosophers_discussed.name: John Stuart Mill
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Singled out by Nietzsche for special contempt as 'that blockhead,' representative of an 'ignoble' ethic of reciprocity ('what is right for one man is right for another') that Nietzsche rejects as assuming a false equivalence of value between persons.

philosophers_discussed.name: Bertrand Russell
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presents an extended personal critique of Nietzsche's ethics, staging an imagined debate between Nietzsche and the Buddha and concluding, in his own voice, that he 'dislikes' Nietzsche's philosophy and 'agree[s] with Buddha' as he has imagined him.

core_concepts.name: Will to power
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Nietzsche holds that the deepest drive in human beings -- more fundamental than pleasure, self-preservation, or even truth-seeking -- is the desire for power, for the capacity to overcome resistance, endure hardship, and impose one's will on the world and on others.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Nietzsche's central psychological and ethical category: the drive to power as the fundamental measure of vitality and worth, tested (per Nietzsche's own words quoted by Russell) 'according to the amount of resistance it can offer and the amount of pain and torture it can endure and know how to turn to its own advantage.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It grounds Nietzsche's entire revaluation of values: strength, cruelty, discipline, and the capacity to inflict and endure suffering become goods, while compassion and equality become symptoms of weakness to be overcome.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed across Nietzsche's mature works, especially Beyond Good and Evil and The Will to Power.
examples: 'I do not point to the evil and pain of existence with the finger of reproach, but rather entertain the hope that life may one day become more evil and more full of suffering than it has ever been.'
Nietzsche's hope for 'a new vast aristocracy based upon the most severe self-discipline, in which the will of philosophical men of power and artist-tyrants will be stamped upon thousands of years.'
objections: Russell argues the lust for power Nietzsche endows his superman with is itself, unrecognized by Nietzsche, an outcome of fear: 'those who do not fear their neighbours see no necessity to tyrannize over them.'
competing_positions: Schopenhauer's will, which is metaphysically fundamental but ethically evil, to be renounced rather than affirmed
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Became one of Nietzsche's most widely (and, Russell implies, sometimes crudely) influential ideas among artistic and literary, rather than technical-philosophical, audiences.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly opposed to Christian ethics, which Nietzsche sees as suppressing the will to power in favor of 'slave morality.'

core_concepts.name: The 'noble' man versus 'slave morality'
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Nietzsche distinguishes an aristocratic ethic, fit only for a superior few, that prizes pride, strength, and the capacity for cruelty ('noble' morality) from the morality actually preached by Christianity and democratic movements, which Nietzsche calls 'slave morality' -- a moral code he says was invented by the weak and resentful to tame and control the strong.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Nietzsche's aristocratic ethical framework: true virtue belongs only to a governing minority (the 'noble' man), who recognizes duties only to equals, may act with cruelty toward inferiors, and embodies the incarnate will to power; this is opposed to Christian/democratic 'slave morality,' which Nietzsche diagnoses as the ideological product of resentment among the 'bungled and botched,' aiming to break the spirit of the strong by converting 'their proud assurance into anxiety and conscience-trouble.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is the ethical center of the chapter and the doctrine Russell subjects to the most sustained criticism, since it explicitly denies that 'the happiness of common people is no part of the good per se.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: Beyond Good and Evil and Thus Spake Zarathustra.
examples: Nietzsche calling ordinary human beings 'the bungled and botched'
'No morality is possible without good birth'
The 'noble' man will protect artists and craftsmen while recognizing duties only to equals
objections: Russell: this requires defining the 'superior few' either as congenitally superior (a biological claim Russell treats skeptically) or as products of education/environment (in which case excluding others from the same advantages is hard to justify).
Russell: it never occurred to Nietzsche that his 'noble' man's lust for power is itself rooted in fear, whereas those who have genuinely conquered fear feel no need to tyrannize.
competing_positions: Bentham's principle of the greatest happiness of the greatest number, which Russell notes is compatible with an aristocratic form of government but not with Nietzsche's aristocratic ethic, since Bentham (unlike Nietzsche) holds the happiness of the many is intrinsically good
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes 'many modern developments' connected to this outlook are, in fairness to Nietzsche, 'contrary to his clearly expressed opinions' -- an explicit caution against over-hasty identification of Nietzsche's views with later political movements.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly and extensively targets Christianity as the ideological vehicle of 'slave morality.'

core_concepts.name: Nietzsche's critique of Christianity
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Unlike earlier Enlightenment critics who attacked Christianity for being untrue or for allying with tyranny against the poor, Nietzsche attacks Christianity purely on the grounds of its psychological and social effects: it teaches submission, breaks the spirit of the strong by converting their pride into guilt, and elevates values (humility, pity, equality before God) that Nietzsche regards as symptoms of decay.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Nietzsche's genealogical critique of Christianity as a 'nihilistic' religion (alongside, but worse than, Buddhism in this respect) originating in Jewish resentment and spread by 'holy epileptics' like Saint Paul, which Nietzsche judges not by its metaphysical truth (which he denies of all religions) but by its social effects: taming the strong, converting proud self-assurance into 'anxiety and conscience-trouble,' and thereby working, in spirit, toward the same egalitarian end as the French Revolution and Socialism, which Nietzsche also opposes.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It represents Nietzsche's most historically influential contribution outside professional philosophy, and Russell judges it 'at their best' in a passage on Pascal that he quotes at length and treats as genuinely eloquent, even while rejecting Nietzsche's conclusion.
core_concepts.historical_origin: The Genealogy of Morals, The Antichrist, Beyond Good and Evil.
examples: 'The New Testament is the gospel of a completely ignoble species of man.'
Nietzsche's admiring-yet-damning passage on Pascal as the 'most famous example' of a strong spirit destroyed by Christian self-contempt
objections: Russell: it does not occur to Nietzsche that a person could genuinely, spontaneously feel universal love rather than merely performing love out of fear of retaliation, because Nietzsche himself 'feels almost universal hatred and fear.'

Russell distinguishes two types of saint -- 'the saint by nature' (spontaneous love) and 'the saint from fear' -- and argues Nietzsche can only conceive of the second, illegitimately generalizing his own psychology onto all religious virtue.
competing_positions: The French philosophes' earlier critique of Christianity, which attacked it as untrue and as allied with tyranny -- a critique Russell notes proceeds on entirely different (truth- and justice-based) grounds than Nietzsche's purely psychological/social one
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Shaped a durable current of anti-Christian cultural criticism distinct from Enlightenment rationalist critique.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central: the entire concept is a critique of Christianity's social and psychological effects.

core_concepts.name: Nietzsche's contempt for women
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Nietzsche repeatedly and harshly disparages women, treating them as incapable of friendship, existing chiefly for men's 'recreation,' and dangerous once granted independence from male control; Russell treats this less as a serious argument than as a revealing symptom of Nietzsche's own psychology.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A recurring element of Nietzsche's ethics, expressed in passages from Thus Spake Zarathustra ('Man shall be trained for war and woman for the recreation of the warrior') and Beyond Good and Evil (recommending women be regarded 'as property, as Orientals do'), offered by Nietzsche as self-evident rather than argued from evidence.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell uses it as a case study in how Nietzsche's stated doctrines can be read as 'objectification[s] of his own emotion,' arguing Nietzsche's fierce misogyny masks fear -- 'nine women out of ten would get the whip away from him, and he knew it.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: Thus Spake Zarathustra, Beyond Good and Evil, The Will to Power.
examples: 'Thou goest to woman? Do not forget thy whip.'
Women described as 'not, as yet, capable of friendship; they are still cats, or birds, or at best cows.'
objections: Russell: 'it is not backed up by evidence from history or from his own experience, which, so far as women were concerned, was almost confined to his sister.'

core_concepts.name: Nietzsche and Machiavelli compared
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell finds a deep affinity between Nietzsche's philosophy and Machiavelli's The Prince: both propose an ethic aimed at power and deliberately opposed to Christian morality, even though Machiavelli was a practical statesman writing from direct political experience while Nietzsche was an academic philologist working out a systematic, bookish philosophy in conscious opposition to his age.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's comparative thesis: Nietzsche's political philosophy is 'analogous to that of The Prince (not The Discourses),' sharing with Machiavelli an ethic aimed at power and deliberately anti-Christian, though worked out more systematically and over a wider field by Nietzsche, and differing in that Machiavelli was a non-systematic man of affairs in harmony with his age, while Nietzsche was a bookish professor consciously opposed to the dominant political and ethical trends of his time.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It situates Nietzsche within a longer Western tradition of frankly power-centered political ethics rather than treating him as a wholly novel phenomenon.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Russell's comparative analysis in this chapter.
core_concepts.associated_philosopher: Friedrich Nietzsche, compared to Niccolò Machiavelli
examples: Russell's formula: 'What Caesar Borgia was to Machiavelli, Napoleon was to Nietzsche: a great man defeated by petty opponents.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Both figures' ethics are explicitly anti-Christian and power-oriented.

arguments.title: Nietzsche's argument against Christian/utilitarian reciprocity ethics
premises: Principles like 'what is right for one man is right for another' or 'do not to others that which you would not that they should do unto you' treat all human traffic as reducible to an exchange of mutual services, as though every action were a cash payment.
This hypothesis assumes an equivalence of value between the actions (and, implicitly, the persons) involved.
arguments.conclusion: Such principles are 'ignoble to the last degree,' since there is in fact no such equivalence of value between the actions of different persons -- specifically, between the actions of superior and inferior men.
arguments.explanation: Russell quotes this argument (directed explicitly at John Stuart Mill, whom Nietzsche calls 'that blockhead') as exemplary of Nietzsche's rejection of universalist, egalitarian ethics in favor of an aristocratic hierarchy of value.
objections: Russell treats this as resting on an unargued assumption -- that some persons' actions/interests are simply worth more than others' -- which he examines at length in the chapter's final section on aristocratic versus democratic ethics.
implications: Grounds Nietzsche's broader claim that the happiness of ordinary people is 'no part of the good per se,' and that only the excellence of a superior few has intrinsic value.

arguments.title: Russell's reconstruction of Nietzsche's ethical syllogism
premises: Victors in war, and their biological descendants, are usually superior (in Nietzsche's specific sense: more strength of will, courage, impulse toward power, less sympathy, less fear) to the vanquished.
It is desirable that the biologically superior should hold power and manage affairs in their own interest.
arguments.conclusion: Aristocracy -- rule by a conquering, biologically superior minority -- is ethically desirable, and the happiness of the majority counts for nothing intrinsically.
arguments.explanation: Russell reconstructs this as 'a fair analysis' of Nietzsche's ethic, then interrogates the crucial and undefended term 'desirable,' arguing that from an outsider's point of view Nietzsche's 'desirable' collapses into 'desired by Nietzsche himself,' which Russell says could be stated more honestly as the autobiographical sentence: 'I wish I had lived in the Athens of Pericles or the Florence of the Medici.'
objections: Russell: the word 'desirable' is not synonymous with 'desired by me'; it claims (however shadowy) legislative universality that Nietzsche's naturalistic ethic cannot supply, since he cannot appeal to God's desires (as a theist could) nor consistently to Kantian ethical intuition (which 'sounds too Kantian').
implications: Leads Russell into the chapter's climactic staged debate between Nietzsche and the Buddha over whether an aristocratic or a universally sympathetic ethic can be defended to an impartial listener.

arguments.title: The imagined debate between Nietzsche and the Buddha
premises: Buddha's case: the world is full of suffering (lepers, the poor, the wounded, orphans, even the successful haunted by fear of failure and death), and a way of salvation, found through love, must be sought for all of it.

Nietzsche's case: trivial and great sufferings alike are not to be regretted when they are noble; Nietzsche has positive ideals (Alcibiades, Frederick II, Napoleon) for whose sake 'any misery is worth while,' and Buddha's ideal (absence of suffering) is merely negative, achievable by non-existence.

Buddha's reply: his ideal is not merely negative -- it includes positive goods (his successor Jesus's command to love enemies, the discovery of ways to master nature and reduce disease, the beauty found by poets and artists) fully comparable to anything in Nietzsche's doctrine.
arguments.conclusion: Russell states his own verdict directly: 'For my part, I agree with Buddha as I have imagined him,' while acknowledging 'I do not know how to prove that he is right by any argument such as can be used in a mathematical or a scientific question.'
arguments.explanation: This staged dialogue is Russell's most explicit and personal statement in the chapter, deliberately marked (via 'as I have imagined him' and the first-person 'I agree') as his own value judgment rather than a claim to logical proof, and it functions as the chapter's rhetorical climax.
implications: Russell concludes the ultimate argument against an internally consistent but unpleasant ethic like Nietzsche's lies 'not in an appeal to facts, but in an appeal to the emotions' -- an explicit acknowledgment that his rejection of Nietzsche rests on value, not on strict logical refutation.

key_distinctions: Nietzsche's will-to-power ethics (will has both metaphysical and ethical primacy) vs. Schopenhauer's (will is metaphysically fundamental but ethically evil)
An aristocratic ethic (value resides only in the superior few) vs. an aristocratic political theory compatible with a democratic/universalist ethic (e.g., Bentham)
'Desirable' as claiming universal, legislative authority vs. 'desirable' collapsing into merely 'desired by me'
The saint by nature (spontaneous love) vs. the saint from fear (virtue only from dread of punishment)
An aristocratic political theory (about who should govern) vs. an aristocratic ethical theory (about whose happiness intrinsically matters)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Nietzsche is presented as Schopenhauer's direct successor (correcting Schopenhauer's inconsistency between a voluntarist metaphysics and an ascetic ethic), as continuing Byron's 'aristocratic rebel' posture (discussed two chapters earlier) into full philosophical form, as an admirer of the pre-Socratics (especially Heraclitus) while harshly rejecting Socrates and Plato, and as closely comparable to Machiavelli in political outlook.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell notes Nietzsche's doctrine of the primacy of will was carried forward by Bergson, James, and Dewey (introduced in the previous chapter), though Russell explicitly cautions that 'many modern developments' connected to Nietzsche's outlook are 'contrary to his clearly expressed opinions,' an implicit but pointed warning against simplistic identification of Nietzsche with later fascist appropriation of his ideas.
political_social_context: The chapter directly engages nationalism, aristocracy versus democracy, and the politics of the era in which Russell writes (1945): Russell notes Nietzsche's prophecies of an era of great wars proved 'more nearly right than those of liberals or Socialists,' and closes with a sustained comparison of aristocratic political forms (Fascist and Nazi parties as the only 'practicable form of aristocracy' available in the modern world) to their historical predecessors.
religion_science_culture_context: Extensive engagement with Christianity (contrasted with Buddhism), and with Nietzsche's own religious upbringing as a pastor's son, his rejection of Christian metaphysics on social/psychological rather than truth-value grounds, and his notably qualified relationship to Judaism (not straightforwardly anti-Semitic in Russell's account, admiring the Old Testament while rejecting the New).
russell_presentation: Russell presents Nietzsche as more consistent and coherent than Schopenhauer, systematically reconstructing his ethics of the 'noble' man, his will to power, his critique of Christian 'slave morality,' his contempt for women, and his comparison to Machiavelli, with extensive direct quotation. Russell is explicit throughout that Nietzsche's importance is primarily ethical and as 'an acute historical critic,' not as an inventor of new technical philosophy. Russell's own editorial voice becomes especially pronounced in the chapter's final third: he calls much of Nietzsche 'merely megalomaniac,' diagnoses Nietzsche's misogyny and will-to-power ethics as themselves rooted in fear (an irony Nietzsche 'never' recognized), and stages an extended imagined dialogue between Nietzsche and the Buddha before declaring outright, in the first person, that he 'dislike[s]' Nietzsche's philosophy and sides with the Buddha -- while candidly admitting this preference rests on 'an appeal to the emotions' rather than strict proof. Russell also takes care to note, in fairness to Nietzsche, that Nietzsche was 'not definitely anti-Semitic' in the way later movements were, was not a German nationalist, and that many later political movements associated with his name diverge from his actual, explicit views -- distinctions a careful reader should keep separate from Russell's harsh ethical verdict on Nietzsche's own stated doctrines.
critical_context: Common scholarly caveat, worth flagging explicitly for a modern reader: Nietzsche scholarship after Russell's time has argued at length that Nietzsche's posthumous association with Nazism was substantially the product of selective, distorting editing of his notebooks by his sister Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche (who compiled The Will to Power and had her own antisemitic and nationalist sympathies, which Nietzsche himself explicitly rejected), and that Nietzsche's actual texts are considerably more ambiguous, ironic, and resistant to straightforward political appropriation than a chapter written in 1945 -- in the immediate aftermath of the Second World War, with Nazism as the still-live political reference point -- was well positioned to register. Russell himself partially anticipates this caution (noting Nietzsche's explicit rejection of German nationalism and of straightforward anti-Semitism), but the chapter's overall rhetorical arc nonetheless treats Nietzsche as a genuine, dangerous precursor of the politics Russell had just seen defeated, a reading later specialists (e.g., Walter Kaufmann's influential mid-twentieth-century rehabilitation of Nietzsche) have substantially contested as insufficiently attentive to irony, literary style, and the difference between Nietzsche's texts and their subsequent political use.
key_takeaways: Nietzsche regarded himself as Schopenhauer's successor, correcting what he saw as an inconsistency between Schopenhauer's voluntarist metaphysics and his ethic of ascetic renunciation by giving will both metaphysical and ethical primacy.

Nietzsche's central ethical doctrine distinguishes 'noble' morality (aristocratic, power-oriented, fit only for a superior few) from Christian/democratic 'slave morality,' which he diagnoses as the resentful invention of the weak to tame the strong.
Nietzsche criticizes Christianity not on grounds of truth (he thinks no religion is true) but purely by its social and psychological effects, judging it as breaking the spirit of the strong.

Russell compares Nietzsche extensively to Machiavelli: both hold power-centered, deliberately anti-Christian ethics, though Machiavelli was a practical statesman and Nietzsche a bookish philologist-professor.

Russell's central objection is that Nietzsche never recognizes that the will to power he prizes is itself rooted in fear, and that Nietzsche can only imagine 'the saint from fear,' never the saint whose love and restraint are spontaneous.

Russell closes with an explicit, first-person value judgment -- staged as an imagined debate between Nietzsche and the Buddha -- siding with the Buddha's ethic of universal sympathy, while candidly acknowledging this preference rests on an appeal to emotion rather than strict logical proof.
study_notes:
This chapter rewards being read in two registers simultaneously: as faithful exposition of Nietzsche's actual doctrines (his will to power, his 'noble man,' his critique of Christianity, his views on women, his comparison to Machiavelli -- all reported with direct quotation and textual citation) and as an increasingly explicit statement of Russell's own ethical and political values, especially in the chapter's final third. A careful student should be able to separate these two registers cleanly: what does Nietzsche actually say (reportable, quotable, Layer 1), and where does Russell step forward to evaluate, criticize, or emotionally reject what Nietzsche says (clearly Russell's own argued position, not a neutral report)? Russell himself models this separation by using explicit first-person language ('I dislike,' 'For my part, I agree with Buddha,' 'What are we to think of Nietzsche's doctrines?') precisely at the points where he moves from exposition to judgment.

The chapter's single most important philosophical move is Russell's analysis of the word 'desirable' in Nietzsche's ethics: since Nietzsche cannot appeal to God's will (he is an atheist) or to Kantian ethical intuition (which he rejects as sounding too much like the reciprocity ethics he despises), his claim that aristocratic rule is 'desirable' seems to collapse into the autobiographical claim that Nietzsche himself desires it -- which is a fact about Nietzsche, not a philosophical argument with any claim on other people. This is a genuinely serious metaethical challenge (about whether naturalistic, non-universalizable value claims can be more than autobiography) worth understanding on its own terms, independent of whether one finds Nietzsche's substantive ethical views appealing or repugnant.

Finally, note carefully what Russell does and does not claim about Nietzsche's relationship to Nazism: he explicitly states Nietzsche was 'not definitely anti-Semitic' and 'not a nationalist,' and that 'many modern developments' connected with his outlook are 'contrary to his clearly expressed opinions' -- important qualifications that complicate any simple 'Nietzsche caused fascism' reading of the chapter, even though Russell's overall rhetorical arc (writing in 1945) clearly treats Nietzsche's philosophy as dangerously continuous with the politics of the era. This is exactly the kind of Russell editorializing that should be labeled and evaluated as such, not absorbed uncritically as settled historical fact about Nietzsche.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Nietzsche's idea that the deepest human drive is not pleasure or survival but the desire for power -- the capacity to overcome resistance and impose one's will.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Nietzsche's central psychological/ethical category, treating power (measured by the resistance a will can overcome and the suffering it can endure and use to its advantage) as the fundamental measure of vitality and value.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Nietzsche's name for the morality of pity, humility, and equality he associates with Christianity and democracy, which he claims was invented by the weak to control and tame the strong.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Nietzsche's genealogical category for a morality he attributes to resentment among the weak ('the bungled and botched'), which elevates values like compassion and equality precisely because they check and morally discredit the power of the strong.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Nietzsche's ideal aristocratic type: capable of cruelty when necessary, recognizing duties only to equals, and embodying strength of will rather than sympathy or humility.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Nietzsche's positive ethical ideal, replacing the Christian saint: a governing-aristocrat type who recognizes duties only toward equals, protects and patronizes artists and skilled craftsmen from a position of superiority, and is essentially defined as the incarnate will to power.

glossary_terms.term: The saint by nature vs. the saint from fear
glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Russell's distinction between someone who is genuinely, spontaneously kind because it makes them happy, and someone who only avoids wrongdoing because they fear punishment (from God, hell, or their neighbors).
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's critical distinction, introduced to diagnose a limit in Nietzsche's psychology: Nietzsche, being full of fear and hatred, can only conceive of virtue as fear-motivated restraint ('the saint from fear'), and cannot imagine spontaneous, fearless, non-self-interested love as a real possibility ('the saint by nature').

questions.prompt: How does Nietzsche's relationship to will differ from Schopenhauer's, according to Russell?
questions.answer: Schopenhauer makes will metaphysically fundamental but ethically evil -- an inconsistent combination, Russell says, given Schopenhauer's oriental ethic of renunciation sits oddly with his metaphysic of the omnipotence of will. Nietzsche corrects this by giving will both metaphysical and ethical primacy: the will to power is not only fundamental but genuinely good, to be affirmed and intensified rather than renounced.
questions.explanation: This distinction is the chapter's opening move and explains why Russell regards Nietzsche as more internally consistent than Schopenhauer, whatever his other objections.

questions.prompt: What is Nietzsche's distinction between 'noble' morality and 'slave morality,' and which does he associate with Christianity?
questions.answer: 'Noble' morality is Nietzsche's aristocratic ideal, fit only for a superior minority: it prizes pride, strength, and even cruelty, and recognizes duties only toward equals. 'Slave morality' -- which Nietzsche associates with Christianity and democracy -- is a morality of pity, humility, and equality that Nietzsche diagnoses as the resentful invention of the weak ('the bungled and botched') to tame and control the strong.
questions.explanation: This distinction organizes Nietzsche's whole revaluation of values and his critique of both Christianity and modern democratic/socialist movements.

questions.prompt: Compare Nietzsche's critique of Christianity to that of the earlier French philosophes, as Russell presents the contrast.
questions.answer: The French philosophes criticized Christianity as untrue, as teaching submission to a supposed divine will that self-respecting people should not accept, and as an ally of tyrants against the poor and against democracy. Nietzsche, by contrast, is not interested in whether Christianity (or any religion) is metaphysically true; he judges it entirely by its social and psychological effects, and he explicitly rejects the philosophes' claim that Christianity allies with tyranny -- he argues the reverse, that Christianity (like the French Revolution and Socialism) is essentially on the side of the weak against the strong.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this contrast to sharpen exactly what is distinctive -- and, in his view, more radical -- about Nietzsche's anti-Christian critique.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's analysis of the word 'desirable' in Nietzsche's ethics, and explain why Russell thinks it poses a problem for Nietzsche.
questions.answer: Nietzsche claims aristocratic rule by the biologically superior is 'desirable,' but since Nietzsche is an atheist he cannot ground this in God's desires (as a theist could), and he will not appeal to ethical intuition because it 'sounds too Kantian.' Russell argues that, from an outsider's standpoint, 'desirable' in Nietzsche's mouth collapses into 'desired by Nietzsche' -- which could be honestly restated as the autobiographical sentence 'I wish I had lived in the Athens of Pericles or the Florence of the Medici,' a fact about Nietzsche's temperament rather than a philosophical claim with authority over other people's values.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's central metaethical challenge to Nietzsche, questioning whether his naturalistic ethic can claim any genuine universality.

questions.prompt: What does Russell say Nietzsche 'never' recognized about the will to power he attributes to his ideal 'superman'?
questions.answer: Russell argues Nietzsche never recognized that the lust for power he endows his superman with is itself an outcome of fear -- 'those who do not fear their neighbours see no necessity to tyrannize over them' -- and that Nietzsche's 'artist-tyrant' figures resemble frightened despots (like Nero) rather than genuinely fearless men.
questions.explanation: This is one of Russell's sharpest psychological reversals of Nietzsche's own diagnostic method (Nietzsche accuses Christian love of masking fear; Russell turns the same tool back on Nietzsche's will to power).

questions.prompt: In Russell's imagined debate, what positive (not merely negative) goods does the Buddha claim for his own ethic, in response to Nietzsche's charge that Buddhism offers only the absence of suffering?
questions.answer: The Buddha replies that his ideal includes positive elements fully comparable to Nietzsche's: heroes such as his successor Jesus (who told men to love their enemies), those who discovered how to master nature and reduce labor, physicians who diminish disease, and poets, artists, and musicians who capture glimpses of divine beauty -- concluding that 'love and knowledge and delight in beauty are not negations; they are enough to fill the lives of the greatest men that have ever lived.'
questions.explanation: This exchange is Russell's direct rebuttal, via the imagined Buddha, to Nietzsche's charge that a sympathy-based ethic is merely negative.

questions.prompt: Despite his overall harsh judgment, what two qualifications does Russell explicitly make in Nietzsche's favor regarding nationalism and antisemitism?
questions.answer: Russell states Nietzsche 'is not a nationalist, and shows no excessive admiration for Germany,' instead wanting an international ruling race; and that Nietzsche 'is also not definitely anti-Semitic,' admiring the Old Testament while disliking the New, though he did think Germany contained as many Jews as it could assimilate. Russell adds that 'many modern developments' connected with Nietzsche's outlook are 'contrary to his clearly expressed opinions.'
questions.explanation: These qualifications complicate any simple equation of Nietzsche's actual views with the nationalist, antisemitic politics of the era in which Russell is writing.

flashcards.front: In what way does Nietzsche correct what he saw as Schopenhauer's inconsistency?
flashcards.back: By giving will both metaphysical AND ethical primacy, rather than making will fundamental but ethically evil (as Schopenhauer does).

flashcards.front: What is Nietzsche's term for the morality of pity, humility, and equality he associates with Christianity and democracy?
What does Nietzsche call ordinary human beings, expressing his contempt for the masses?
Which English philosopher does Nietzsche single out for special contempt as 'that blockhead'?
What famous aphorism does Nietzsche give about approaching women?
flashcards.back: 'Thou goest to woman? Do not forget thy whip.'

flashcards.front: Whose ethic does Russell compare Nietzsche's political philosophy to at length, and via which specific work?
flashcards.back: Niccolò Machiavelli's, specifically The Prince (not The Discourses).

flashcards.front: What figure was Napoleon to Nietzsche, in Russell's formula pairing Nietzsche with Machiavelli?
flashcards.back: What Caesar Borgia was to Machiavelli, Napoleon was to Nietzsche -- a great man defeated by petty opponents.

flashcards.front: On what grounds does Nietzsche judge religions, rather than their metaphysical truth?
Which philosopher's suffering does Nietzsche cite as 'the most famous example' of Christianity destroying a strong spirit?
What two types of 'saint' does Russell distinguish in his critique of Nietzsche?
flashcards.back: The saint by nature (spontaneous love) and the saint from fear (virtue only from dread of punishment) -- Russell argues Nietzsche can only imagine the second.

flashcards.front: In Russell's analysis, what does Nietzsche's claim that aristocracy is 'desirable' collapse into, since he rejects both theism and Kantian intuition as grounds?
flashcards.back: Essentially, 'desired by Nietzsche himself' -- an autobiographical fact, not a universalizable ethical claim.

flashcards.front: Who does Russell imagine debating Nietzsche before God in the chapter's climactic passage?
What is Russell's final, explicit personal verdict on the Nietzsche/Buddha debate he imagines?
flashcards.back: 'For my part, I agree with Buddha as I have imagined him,' though Russell admits this cannot be proven like a mathematical or scientific claim.

flashcards.front: What two qualifications does Russell make in Nietzsche's favor regarding nationalism and antisemitism?
flashcards.back: Nietzsche was not a German nationalist and was 'not definitely anti-Semitic,' admiring the Old Testament and disliking only the New.

quiz.prompt: How does Nietzsche's treatment of Will differ from Schopenhauer's, according to Russell?
options: Nietzsche denies the existence of will entirely
Nietzsche gives will both metaphysical and ethical primacy, rather than making it fundamental but evil
Nietzsche agrees completely with Schopenhauer on every point
Nietzsche replaces will with pure reason as the fundamental category
quiz.explanation: Schopenhauer made will metaphysically fundamental but ethically evil; Nietzsche gives will ethical as well as metaphysical primacy, correcting what he saw as an inconsistency.

quiz.prompt: What does Nietzsche call the morality of pity, humility, and equality that he associates with Christianity and democracy?
quiz.explanation: Nietzsche's term 'slave morality' names the morality he attributes to resentment among the weak, aimed at taming the strong.

quiz.prompt: True or False: Nietzsche judges Christianity primarily on the grounds that its doctrines are factually untrue.
quiz.explanation: Nietzsche is not interested in the metaphysical truth of Christianity or any religion; being convinced no religion is really true, he judges all religions entirely by their social effects.

quiz.prompt: Which earlier political philosopher does Russell compare Nietzsche to at length, specifically citing which of that philosopher's works?
quiz.explanation: Russell draws a sustained comparison between Nietzsche's ethic aimed at power and Machiavelli's The Prince specifically (not The Discourses).

quiz.prompt: Fill in the blank: Nietzsche calls ordinary human beings, whose suffering he considers acceptable if necessary for producing a great man, 'the ___ and botched.'
quiz.explanation: Nietzsche's phrase 'the bungled and botched' expresses his contempt for ordinary people relative to the excellence of the superior few.

quiz.prompt: What does Russell argue Nietzsche's claim that aristocracy is 'desirable' effectively collapses into, given that Nietzsche rejects both theism and Kantian intuition as grounds?
options: An autobiographical statement of what Nietzsche himself desires
quiz.explanation: Russell argues that without an appeal to God's will or ethical intuition, Nietzsche's 'desirable' can only mean 'desired by Nietzsche' -- a fact about his own temperament, not a claim with authority over others.
quiz.related_concept: Russell's reconstruction of Nietzsche's ethical syllogism

quiz.prompt: True or False: Russell explicitly states that Nietzsche was a German nationalist and straightforwardly anti-Semitic.
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly says Nietzsche 'is not a nationalist, and shows no excessive admiration for Germany,' and 'is also not definitely anti-Semitic,' admiring the Old Testament.

quiz.prompt: Match each figure to their role in Russell's imagined debate and critique: (1) the Buddha, (2) Pascal, (3) Lincoln, (4) John Stuart Mill
options: (a) called 'that blockhead' by Nietzsche for reciprocity ethics; (b) cited by Nietzsche as the 'most famous example' of Christianity destroying a strong spirit; (c) debates Nietzsche in Russell's imagined dialogue; (d) judged 'abject' by Nietzsche despite acting without fear of hell, per Russell
quiz.explanation: Buddha (c): debates Nietzsche; Pascal (b): Nietzsche's example of Christianity destroying strength; Lincoln (d): judged abject by Nietzsche despite fearless virtue; Mill (a): called 'that blockhead.'
quiz.related_concept: The imagined debate between Nietzsche and the Buddha

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's key psychological reversal of Nietzsche's own critical method, applied back against Nietzsche's will to power?
options: That the will to power is scientifically impossible
That the lust for power Nietzsche admires is itself, like the Christian love Nietzsche dismisses as fear-based, rooted in fear
That Nietzsche secretly believed in God
That will to power is identical to Schopenhauer's Will
quiz.explanation: Just as Nietzsche argues Christian love masks fear of retaliation, Russell argues Nietzsche's own prized will to power masks a deeper fear -- those who have truly conquered fear feel no need to tyrannize over others.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, on what basis does he ultimately reject Nietzsche's philosophy, given that he admits it is internally consistent?
options: A mathematical proof of its falsehood
An appeal to the emotions, since Nietzsche despises universal love while Russell feels it 'the motive power to all that I desire as regards the world'
A scientific experiment disproving the will to power
Nietzsche's own later insanity discredits the philosophy
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly states that the ultimate argument against an unpleasant but internally self-consistent ethic like Nietzsche's lies 'not in an appeal to facts, but in an appeal to the emotions.'
quiz.related_concept: The imagined debate between Nietzsche and the Buddha

essay_prompts.prompt: Analyze Russell's critique of the word 'desirable' in Nietzsche's ethics. Does Russell succeed in showing that Nietzsche's aristocratic ethic collapses into mere autobiography, or can a defender of Nietzsche resist this move?
rubric: Explains why Nietzsche cannot appeal to theism or Kantian intuition
Considers a plausible Nietzschean response (e.g., a naturalistic account of value)

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's claim that Nietzsche's will to power is itself, unrecognized by Nietzsche, rooted in fear. Is this a fair philosophical criticism, or does it merely turn Nietzsche's own diagnostic style back on him without independent support?
rubric: States Russell's argument accurately with textual support
Considers whether the argument is falsifiable or merely rhetorical
Engages with Nietzsche's own texts on fear/strength where relevant

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare the ethical positions Russell assigns to Nietzsche and to the Buddha in the chapter's imagined debate. Whose position do you find more persuasive, and why? Be explicit about which parts of your answer are factual reconstruction of the text and which are your own evaluative judgment.
rubric: Accurately reconstructs both positions from the text
Clearly separates exposition from personal evaluation
Provides reasoned support for the position taken
Engages with Russell's own acknowledgment that this is a matter of value, not proof
